August 29, 2026 — One can scarcely imagine the terror: standing inside your own home, hearing the roar of water, mud, and rocks approaching — and having only seconds to wonder if your family will survive. That was the reality for communities along the Nepal–Tibet border on August 26, 2026, when a massive glacier and rock collapse triggered a catastrophic flash flood along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi rivers. Homes, roads, bridges, power plants, and entire settlements were swept away — often with little or no warning.  IN THOSE FINAL MOMENTS Residents were forced to scramble to rooftops, balconies, or any higher ground available — clinging to hope as waters rose nearly 30 feet in half an hour. We may never fully know what went through their minds: Were they crying? Calling loved ones? Praying? Holding each other? What we do know is that behind every statistic is a human life, a family, and a story of heartbreak.  THE SCALE OF LOSS - 469 confirmed dead — and still rising - Hundreds more remain missing, including tourists and pilgrims from several nations - Entire communities buried under mud and debris - Rescue teams continue to reach isolated areas "Behind every number is a family waiting. Behind every missing person is someone desperately hoping. And behind every survivor is a story of courage."  May rescuers reach those still waiting. May the missing be found. And may every grieving family find strength in this time of unimaginable loss.  ,///Charlie. #PrayForNepal #NepalFlood #HimalayanDisaster #FlashFlood #DisasterAwareness #HopeAndPrayer #BosesNgPilipinas See less LOOK:|BEHIND EVERY NUMBER: THE HUMAN HEARTBREAK OF NEPAL’S FLASH FLOOD.

#1DNews | Davao, Philippines  FLOOD ALERT | Street Flooding Hits Carmelite Area in Bajada Following Hours of Rain LOOK: Residents of the Carmelite area in Bajada, Davao City, experienced street flooding early Wednesday, July 1, after several hours of continuous rainfall overnight. According to residents, flooding in the area is a recurring problem whenever heavy rains persist for more than two hours. As of this morning, floodwaters had reportedly risen from knee to waist level in some sections, affecting road access and threatening nearby homes, vehicles, and other properties. While residents noted that floodwaters typically recede within two to three hours after the rain stops, many continue to express concern over the recurring flooding and the damage it brings to their belongings and daily activities. Authorities are advising motorists and the public to exercise caution when passing through flood-prone areas. Warning Signs: Two Major Drug Busts Show The Philippines Is Being Targeted Two massive drug seizures in neighboring countries are sounding a clear alarm: the Philippines is being directly targeted by major drug syndicates, and we cannot afford to ignore the risk.  Bust #1: 521 KG of Meth Seized From Private Jet in Laos October 1, 2026 At Luang Prabang International Airport, Laotian authorities intercepted a private jet carrying a staggering 521 kilograms of methamphetamine — packed into 21 suitcases. Malaysia’s Narcotics Crime Investigation Department confirmed the drugs came from Laos and were bound for Manila, Philippines. Thirteen people were arrested — including a Singaporean pilot, a Malaysian co-pilot, a Filipino passenger, and Laotian nationals. This wasn’t a small-time operation; it was a sophisticated, international delivery flying straight to our shores.  Bust #2: Over 1 Tonne of Ice Seized in Gulf of Thailand, Headed for PH October 8, 2026 Thai Marine Police and the Narcotics Suppression Division intercepted a vessel in the lower Gulf of Thailand after careful surveillance. Hidden in a secret compartment at the stern, they found 1,178 kilograms of crystal methamphetamine ("ice") — packed into 39 sacks. Police confirmed the vessel was actively preparing to transport the shipment to the Philippines. That’s over 1.1 tonnes of dangerous drugs — enough to flood communities and destroy countless lives.  The Bigger Picture These aren’t isolated incidents. In just one week, nearly 1.7 tonnes of meth bound for the Philippines was intercepted outside our borders. It shows our country is being targeted by large-scale, well-organized drug networks. This is exactly why we must take the risk of narco-state tendencies seriously. When powerful syndicates treat our nation as a primary destination for their shipments, it threatens our communities, our youth, and our institutions. The drugs may have been seized abroad — but the warning is for us. We need stronger border intelligence, better regional coordination, and greater vigilance at home. Let’s not wait until these shipments start arriving successfully. Our safety depends on staying one step ahead.  #NarcoState See less Warning Signs: Two Major Drug Busts Show The Philippines Is Being Targeted

Hurricane Isaias has strengthened to 110 mph, placing it just below Category 3 intensity on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale. According to the National Hurricane Center’s 4:00 AM advisory, Hurricane Hunter aircraft indicate that Isaias continues to intensify, and the hurricane is likely to reach major hurricane strength this morning. Although some weakening is forecast before landfall, Isaias is expected to remain a dangerous hurricane capable of producing destructive winds, life-threatening storm surge, flooding rainfall and tornadoes.  The time for hurricane preparations is rapidly running out across portions of the northern Gulf Coast. ⸻  LATEST HURRICANE INFORMATION — 4:00 AM CDT *   Maximum sustained winds: 110 mph, with higher gusts. *   Minimum central pressure: 963 millibars. *   Location: 26.4°N, 88.0°W. *   Movement: North-northeast at 15 mph. *   Distance: Approximately 200 miles south-southeast of the mouth of the Mississippi River. *   Hurricane-force winds: Extend outward up to 30 miles from the center. *   Tropical-storm-force winds: Extend outward up to 185 miles from the center. *   Aircraft reconnaissance: Air Force and NOAA Hurricane Hunters confirm strengthening. DAVAO: THE “FLOOD CAPITAL” — BUT PERHAPS NOT FOR THE REASON YOU THINK They say Davao is the “Flood Capital of the Philippines.” Well, if someone insists on giving us that crown, perhaps we should wear it proudly—but let’s first ask a simple question: What exactly is overflowing?  Yes, Davao experiences floods. We have rivers that swell after relentless rain, low-lying communities that sometimes bear the brunt of nature, sudden downpours that seem to arrive without an appointment, and roads that occasionally transform into temporary swimming pools. That is a real problem. It deserves real solutions—not political theater. But if we are going to compare cities, perhaps the scoreboard deserves more than a political slogan. During the severe southwest monsoon flooding in July 2025, for example, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority reported hundreds of flooding incidents across Metro Manila within a single day. So before anyone points a finger at Davao, perhaps we should remember that flooding is not a problem exclusive to one city. Water does not check political affiliations before it rises. Rain does not ask who you voted for before it pours. And rivers certainly don't read campaign speeches.  But here's where I see Davao differently. Because there is another kind of flooding happening here—one that doesn't destroy homes, close roads, or leave mud behind. Davao floods with culture. Walk through this city and you encounter a living mosaic of Mindanao: Indigenous traditions, migrant communities, different languages, cuisines, beliefs, stories, and histories woven together into one constantly evolving urban tapestry. Ask someone where they came from, and you may discover an entire story behind the answer. Then, inevitably, there's food. Because in Davao, you can start a conversation about almost anything and somehow end up discussing durian.  “This variety is sweeter.” “No, that one has better texture.” “You haven't tried the best one yet.” Suddenly, what began as a casual conversation has transformed into an international conference on durian. No registration fee required.  But perhaps Davao's most remarkable flood is neither water nor culture. It is warmth. There is a quiet generosity in the character of many Dabawenyos that statistics cannot measure. You can arrive as a stranger and, before long, someone may already be telling you where to eat, what places to visit, which shortcut to take—and, most importantly, which road to avoid when traffic is terrible. That's not just hospitality. That's hospitality with a built-in traffic advisory.  And then there is Davao's natural beauty. The sea. Samal. Mount Apo. The forests. The farms. The rivers. The mountains. The wide spaces that remind you that progress and nature do not always have to be enemies. Davao is also changing. Businesses are arriving. Buildings are rising. Infrastructure is expanding. Communities are growing. People continue to come—not only because they are looking for jobs, but because they are looking for possibilities. Some arrive carrying résumés. Others arrive carrying business plans. Some arrive carrying nothing more than a dream. And somewhere along the way, many discover something unexpected: They don't merely live in Davao. They become part of it. That, perhaps, is the real story. A city should not be judged solely by the problems that rise within it. It should also be judged by what its people continue to build despite those problems. Davao is not perfect. We have traffic. We have growing pains. We have environmental concerns. We have infrastructure challenges. We have political disagreements. And, of course, we have social-media experts who can apparently repair the entire country using nothing but a smartphone and a Facebook account.  But beneath all the noise is something far more difficult to construct: Character. You can build a highway. You can build skyscrapers. You can build malls, bridges, offices, and massive developments. You can even build a spectacular roundabout that everyone will complain about for months.  But you cannot manufacture belonging. You cannot pour it into concrete. You cannot buy it from a catalog. It has to grow. And Davao has grown through people. People from different places came here. They planted roots. They built families. They opened businesses. They raised children. They created communities. And little by little, their individual stories became part of the larger story of the city. For the past 15 years, I have had the privilege of traveling around Davao for team-building activities, retreats, seminars, workshops, and speaking engagements. And in those years, I have seen something that no flood statistics can capture. I have seen people flood others with smiles, generosity, and warmth. Noong Setyembre 4, 2026, namahagi ang OVP-DOC ng food packs sa Barangay Mariblo, Quezon City para sa 500 pamilyang nakaranas ng matinding pag-ulan at pagbaha. Ang mga food pack, na mula sa mga donasyon ng mga pribadong indibidwal, ay naglalaman ng tig-5 kilong bigas, de-lata, at ready-to-eat goods. Samantala, noong Setyembre 7, 2026 naman ay naghatid ang OVP-DOC ng food bags sa Calumpit, Bulacan para sa 1,645 pamilyang pansamantalang nananatili sa mga evacuation center. Bawat food bag ay naglalaman ng tig-5 kilong bigas at mga de-latang pagkain. Lubos na nagpapasalamat ang OVP sa mga pribadong indibidwal at iba pang katuwang na partners na patuloy na nakikiisa at nagbibigay-suporta sa mga relief operations para sa mga pamilyang nangangailangan.
